name: Small Hours
tagline: Essays by Maud Ellery on paying attention

els.text: Four minutes is long enough to notice the morning, if you let the kettle set the pace.
I write one essay a month about paying attention: to walks, kettles, old letters and the things people keep. Small Hours is where they live.
One essay a month and nothing else. Follow along in any feed reader, or write to me and I’ll answer.
I was a librarian for fourteen years, which is mostly a job about noticing what people need before they ask. Now I write, slowly, about the small things that hold a day together.
I walk most mornings, keep a commonplace book and answer every letter, eventually. A new essay arrives here on the third Sunday of each month.
Essays have appeared in The Slow Review, Field Notes Quarterly and The Kitchen Table. A small collection, Ordinary Weather, is out from Lantern Press.

sections.heading: Letters are welcome
sections.text: Tell me what you noticed, or what you think I got wrong. I read everything and answer most of it, usually on a Sunday.

posts.title: The kettle and the hour
posts.excerpt: Four minutes is long enough to notice the morning, if you let the kettle set the pace.
posts.content:
My kettle takes four minutes to boil. For years I spent those minutes on my phone, and the morning arrived already full of other people.

Last winter I started standing at the window instead. Nothing much happens out there: a neighbour scrapes his car, a gull complains, the light changes from grey to slightly less grey.

I have not become calmer, or wiser, or better at mornings. But I know what the street looks like at seven in every month of the year now, and that feels like owning something.

The kettle clicks off. I make the tea. The day can come in.

posts.title: On keeping a commonplace book
posts.excerpt: A notebook of other people’s sentences turns out to be a portrait of the person copying them.
posts.content:
A commonplace book is a notebook of things worth keeping: lines from books, overheard remarks, a recipe, the name of a tree. People kept them for centuries before anyone called it a system.

Mine is a green hardback with a broken spine. I copy things out by hand, which is slow, and the slowness is the point. You only copy what you mean to remember.

What ends up in it

Reading it back, I find almost nothing about success and a great deal about weather, walking and kindness from strangers. The book knows what I care about better than I do.

If you start one, start badly. The first page of mine is a bus timetable.

posts.title: Walking the same mile for a year
posts.excerpt: I walked one route every morning for a year. It was a different mile every day.
posts.content:
The rule was simple: the same mile, every morning, from my door to the end of the canal path and back.

By March I knew which bench the heron used and which house fed the foxes. By May I could tell the day of the week from the bins.

People asked if I got bored. I did, in February, for about a week. Then the blackthorn came out and I forgave the whole route.

I have changed routes now. I miss the heron.

posts.title: What the repair shop knows
posts.excerpt: Behind a counter full of broken radios is a whole philosophy of keeping things.
posts.content:
There is a repair shop at the bottom of my road with a hand-painted sign and a counter covered in radios. The man who runs it has been there for thirty-one years.

He told me most things are not broken, only neglected. A loose wire, a dry joint, a fuse nobody thought to check.

I took him my grandmother’s clock. He opened the back, blew on it, and it started ticking. He would not take any money.

I think about that often, and not only about clocks.

posts.title: A defence of the second draft
posts.excerpt: The first draft is for finding out what you think. The second is for the reader.
posts.content:
Every essay on this site was worse the first time. Some of them were much worse.

The first draft is where I find out what I think. It wanders, repeats itself and buries the point in the fourth paragraph.

Where the work is

The second draft is for you. It cuts the throat-clearing, moves the point to the top and takes out the clever sentence I was proud of, because it was only there for me.

There is no third draft. By then I am only moving commas around.

posts.title: Notes from a night bus
posts.excerpt: The last bus home is a small, tired city of its own.
posts.content:
The last bus leaves the centre at twenty past midnight. I took it every Friday for a month and wrote down what I saw.

A nurse asleep against the window with her shoes off. Two students arguing about a film, both wrong. A man carrying a cake, very carefully, all the way to the terminus.

The driver said goodnight to every single passenger. Nobody said it back, and he did not seem to mind.

posts.title: The weather in old letters
posts.excerpt: My grandparents wrote to each other about the weather for forty years. It was never really about the weather.
posts.content:
I found a shoebox of my grandparents’ letters in the loft. Almost every one begins with the weather.

At first this seemed dull. Then I noticed that the weather got worse when one of them was ill, and brighter in the letters after my mother was born.

We think of small talk as empty. I am not sure it ever was.

posts.title: Why I stopped counting books
posts.excerpt: I used to set myself a number of books a year. I read more since I stopped.
posts.content:
For six years I set myself a target: fifty books, then sixty. I hit it every year and remember almost none of them.

Counting made me choose short books, skip the slow ones and abandon nothing, because abandoning did not count.

Last year I read nineteen. I reread two of them straight away. I can tell you what every one of them was about.
